bibliography.abstract: This study investigates the adoption potential of demand-responsive transport (DRT) services in a large UK urban region, with particular emphasis on the role of perceptions toward existing public transport (PT) infrastructure. While DRT is often promoted as a sustainable alternative to conventional modes, its urban implementation in the UK has yielded mixed results, partly due to a limited understanding of behavioral factors that influence its uptake. We employ a hybrid modelling framework combining revealed and stated preference data from 1,490 respondents in the Greater Leeds region, integrating latent perceptions of PT reliability, safety, connectivity, and affordability within a random utility maximisation structure. Unlike traditional integrated choice and latent variable (ICLV) models, we adopt a parsimonious specification using a single-indicator approach, facilitating better interpretability and policy simulation. Our analysis indicates that PT perceptions significantly influence modal preferences, with improvements in safety and connectivity increasing the likelihood of DRT adoption. Notably, these findings challenge the prevailing notion of DRT as a competitor to PT, instead emphasising the complementarity between the two modes. Our policy simulations demonstrate that a balanced “carrot-and-stick” approach--one that simultaneously improves PT infrastructure and service quality while discouraging private car use—can strengthen perceptions of PT, increase its ridership alongside DRT, and ultimately support a modal shift away from private vehicles.

en.caveats: The empirical findings are based on a single urban region in the UK, which may limit generalizability to areas with different baseline transit quality or spatial structures.
en.what: This study models the adoption potential of demand-responsive transport (DRT) using revealed and stated preference data from 1,490 survey respondents in the Greater Leeds region, UK. It employs a parsimonious hybrid choice model with a single-indicator approach to integrate latent perceptions of public transport reliability, safety, connectivity, and affordability. The analysis reveals that positive perceptions of public transport safety and connectivity significantly increase the likelihood of choosing DRT.
en.why: It demonstrates that DRT functions as a complement to, rather than a competitor with, conventional public transit. This allows planners to design 'carrot-and-stick' policies that simultaneously upgrade transit infrastructure and discourage private car use to boost both transit and DRT ridership.
